start.label: Start
start.title: Start
start.line1: You are about to create a new project.
start.line2: We'll guide you step by step through a short series of questions.
start.line3: The questions will be tailored to your methodology and help you:
start.line4: While answering, a virtual assistant will be available to explain each topic.
start.line5: A good first step is to download the PDF form and review it with the team.

list.plan: prepare strong foundations for planning and delivery

criteria.label: Project criteria
criteria.title: Is this a project?
criteria.subtitle: Not everything is a project. Make sure your initiative meets the requirements below.

goal.title: Goal
goal.text: A project has a clear end result, so it is known what exactly will be achieved.

time.title: Temporariness
time.text: A project has a start and an end, so it is not continuous or routine work.

unique.title: Uniqueness
unique.text: A project is unique because its outcome or delivery method is one-off in the given context.

scope.title: Scope of work
scope.text: A project has a defined scope so you know what is in and what is out.

constraints.title: Constraints
constraints.text: A project is delivered within constraints of time, budget, and resources.

team.title: Team / responsibility
team.text: A project has a person or team responsible for delivery and results.

print.title: Project form
print.description: This form helps structure the key project decisions.
print.subtitle: Print this document and fill it out during your team session.

questions.name: What working name best describes the project?
questions.category: What area or theme best fits this project?
questions.goal: What specific, measurable goal do you want to achieve?
questions.outcome: What tangible outcome should be ready at the end?
questions.stakeholders: Who are the stakeholders and what is their impact or interest?
questions.justification: What need or problem does the project address?
questions.mvp: What is the minimum essential scope of the project?
questions.scopeIn: What is included in the project scope?
questions.scopeOut: What is explicitly out of scope?
questions.milestones: Which key milestones will confirm progress?
questions.people: How many people are realistically available to work?
questions.budget: What is the realistic total budget?
questions.chances: What could help the project succeed?
questions.threats: What could make the project harder to deliver?
questions.terms: What are the key dates and what do they mean?

autofill.label: Autofill
autofill.warning: Generated content is often wrong or incomplete ? review and correct it.

expert.body1: The first element is naming the project. This is not a marketing name, but a working name that clearly describes what the project is and its purpose. A good approach is to use a simple, descriptive phrase, e.g.:
expert.list2: Develop and execute a cafe marketing strategy
expert.body2: This keeps the whole team aligned on the goal.

category.title: Project category
category.label: Project category
category.hint: Provide the domain or topic, e.g. IT, marketing, event, process, training.

expert.body: The category helps you understand the main goal and what the team should focus on. For example, for a concert project the right category is event organization; a ticketing app should not be the main focus.

vision.title: Vision
vision.description: At this stage you will define the vision: the goal, why it exists, the expected outcome, and whose needs it addresses.

direction.title: Direction
direction.description: At this stage you will define the key elements of the project, how progress is checked, and plan the most important moments and milestones.

resources.title: Resources
resources.description: At this stage you will define the project resources: people, availability, and the budget needed for delivery.

chances.title: Project opportunities
chances.label: Which elements or factors can help deliver the project?
chances.hint: Type an item and press Enter
chances.empty: Add factors that can realistically support delivery.

expert.body1: Opportunities are internal or external factors that can make delivery easier.
expert.body2: List what increases the chance of success or speeds up the work.

examples.1: ready data or materials from the business team,
examples.3: access to proven vendors or tools.

threats.title: Project threats
threats.label: Which elements or factors can make delivery harder?
threats.hint: Type an item and press Enter
threats.empty: Add factors that can slow down or complicate delivery.

expert.body1: Threats are risks that can delay the project or reduce the quality of the outcome.
expert.body2: List realistic risks that should be monitored and mitigated.

examples.1: lack of availability of key team members,

terms.title: Project dates
terms.label: Dates
terms.hint: e.g. requirements sign-off, kickoff workshop, MVP release
terms.empty: Add key dates with a short description.

expert.body1: Dates describe key moments that affect how the project is delivered.
expert.body2: Pick the dates that set the pace of work or require stakeholder decisions.

wrapup.title: Wrap-up
wrapup.description: At this stage you will close the planning by confirming timelines and reviewing opportunities and threats.

mvp.title: MVP
mvp.label: What must be built for sure?
mvp.hint: Type an item and press Enter
mvp.empty: Add the first MVP items to outline the minimum required.

expert.body1: MVP is the minimum set of elements the project needs to deliver its core function.
expert.body2: Choose only what is absolutely necessary to validate value and measure progress.

examples.1: request form + handling panel (no automation or integrations),
examples.2: simple landing with signup + manual registration handling,
examples.3: basic workflow in an internal tool without reports or analytics.

goal.title: Project goal
goal.label: Describe a concrete, measurable goal you are pursuing in this project.
goal.hint: e.g. improve the effectiveness of identifying infrastructure issues in the city

expert.body: The project goal clearly defines what area or problem will change as a result of the project. It should be unambiguous, precise, and free of vague or conflicting wording.
expert.projectText: What you deliver: the initiative, actions, product, or service.
expert.goalText: Why you do it: the measurable change you want to achieve.

good.1: Public infrastructure issue reporting system - improve identification of infrastructure problems in the city.
good.2: Medical appointment booking app - reduce scheduling time in public health clinics.
good.3: E-learning platform - ensure continuous access to learning materials.
good.4: Waste management system - improve municipal waste segregation effectiveness.

examples.badTitle: ❌ Examples of poorly defined project goals

bad.1: City app - improve quality of life for residents.
bad.3: Online platform - a modern solution for users.

outcome.title: Project outcome
outcome.label: What will be the product/result of your project?
outcome.hint: e.g. a ready app for handling customer requests.

expert.body1: The outcome is a concrete, measurable, tangible end result ready to present, hand over, or implement.
expert.body2: Describe exactly what will be ready after completion. Do not describe actions or methods - focus on the end result.
expert.body3: The outcome should be clear, verifiable, and measurable so there is no doubt the project is complete.

examples.title: Examples
examples.3: a deployed and documented customer service process,
examples.4: a ready application or IT system.

justification.title: Project justification
justification.label: What problems does the project address? / What need does it arise from?
justification.hint: e.g. repeated delays in approval requests between departments.

expert.body1: The project responds to the concrete needs of a specific audience and addresses real problems they face daily. Its justification is the intent to solve identified difficulties and improve the situation of project participants.

examples.1: lack of access to support or services (e.g. limited activity offerings in small towns),
examples.2: insufficient competencies (e.g. lack of digital skills),
examples.3: difficulties in social or professional activation (e.g. long-term unemployed),
examples.4: lack of actions tailored to the specific needs of a given group.

scope.title: Project scope
scope.placeholder: Type an item and press Enter
scope.inHint: What is inside the project scope. Each Enter adds a new item.
scope.outHint: What is outside the project scope. Each Enter adds a new item.

validation.required: Add at least one scope item.

expert.body1: The project scope defines which activities and outcomes are the team's responsibility and which are explicitly excluded.
expert.body2: A precise scope keeps goals clear, prevents uncontrolled expansion, and makes it easier to track progress and evaluate results.
expert.exampleIn: design the layout, implement pages (e.g. home, offer, contact), configure a CMS, run functional tests.
expert.exampleOut: create marketing content, run ad campaigns, long-term maintenance and updates after project completion.

kpi.title: KPI
kpi.label: How will you measure progress?
kpi.hint: Type a metric and press Enter
kpi.empty: Add indicators that show whether the project is moving in the right direction.

expert.body1: KPIs are measurable indicators that show whether the project is on track.
expert.body2: Pick only the ones that truly reflect progress and signal you are getting closer to the goal.

milestones.title: Milestones
milestones.label: What are the most important elements of the project?
milestones.hint: Type a milestone and press Enter
milestones.empty: Add milestones to capture the key moments and deliverables.

expert.body1: Milestones highlight the key elements that confirm the project is progressing in the right direction.
expert.body2: They should be clear, verifiable, and describe tangible checkpoints, not tasks.

people.title: People resources
people.splitHint: Define how many people are often available vs. rarely available on the project.

expert.body1: People resources are the number of people who can realistically support the project within the planned timeframe.
expert.body2: High availability means regular engagement; low availability means occasional support or only in selected stages.

validation.highRequired: Number of people with high availability is required.
validation.lowRequired: Number of people with low availability is required.

budget.title: Total budget
budget.label: Total budget
budget.hint: Enter the planned total budget in PLN, e.g. 5000.

expert.body1: The total budget is the real cost of delivering all planned activities and resources.
expert.body2: Include people costs, tools, materials, vendors, and a buffer for unexpected expenses.
expert.example: e.g. total budget PLN 120,000: team 80,000, tools 15,000, vendors 15,000, contingency 10,000.

expert.body1: No project exists in a vacuum - it always responds to the needs of specific people or groups. Identify stakeholders whose opinions, needs, or decisions can affect delivery.
expert.body2: Think about who should be considered during creation, then place them on the map, considering:
expert.list1: Power - how important a person's opinion is for success (e.g. decision makers like the CEO).
expert.list2: Interest - how much the project addresses real needs and problems of the person or group.
expert.body3: Example: for a ticketing system, Customer Service is a key stakeholder because the project addresses their daily problems and their engagement will be high.

chart.title: Stakeholder map (power - interest)
chart.subtitle: Add a stakeholder and then drag them onto the map.
